speaker: Eric Jang
title: What rebuilding AlphaGo teaches us about self-play, RL, and future of LLMs - Eric Jang
question: In self-play reinforcement learning, why can Monte Carlo tree search produce a worse move distribution than the raw policy network?
guest: In practice, it is a heuristic. Let me illustrate an example where MCTS can give you a worse distribution than your policy network. This can often happen if your self-play algorithm has trained to a good point, but then collapses because it is not trained on diverse data. Suppose we have a board state where the policy recommendations are very good, but because we are playing a lot of games where the bots just resign instead of playing all the way to terminal resolution, they forget how to evaluate late-stage positions. Maybe our replay buffer has lost examples of how to evaluate the value function at those states, so your terminal leaf values become very bad. When the terminal values of the leaves are inaccurate, that error propagates all the way up and causes your PUCT selection criteria and backups to be off, so you end up visiting a very different distribution than what your policy initially recommended. Also, if your number of simulations is low, you get a variance issue where you do not explore enough, since convergence is only guaranteed as simulations approach infinity. So search variance and evaluation inaccuracies can degrade the policy recommendation, which is why improvement is not guaranteed.

points.core: Early game resignations strip terminal examples from the replay buffer.
points.note: Accept: agents resigning early prevents full playouts from entering training data; replay buffer loses endgame resolution coverage. Do not credit: generic claims about needing diverse data without linking early resignation to missing late-stage states.

points.core: Corrupted leaf value estimates propagate upward through backups to distort selection.
points.note: Accept: inaccurate terminal or leaf value predictions corrupt backed-up Q-values and PUCT action selection, steering visit counts away from good moves. Do not credit: merely saying the value function can be wrong without explaining upward tree propagation.

points.core: Too few search simulations introduce high variance before visit counts converge.
points.note: Accept: low simulation budgets cause under-exploration or noisy search estimates since convergence requires large simulation counts. Do not credit: vague mentions of compute limits without linking low simulations to search variance.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
MCTS is only a policy improvement operator when it has enough simulations, and in AlphaZero-style self-play the training target is the root visit-count distribution, which can be a poor estimate when the budget is small.

The main reason is that the PUCT selection rule was designed for exploration, not for producing a good distribution from few visits. With a small simulation budget relative to the number of legal moves, visit counts are coarse and noisy: many good moves get zero visits, and a move can accumulate visits just because of an early optimistic or erroneous value estimate that the search has no time to correct. Dirichlet noise added at the root also forces visits onto moves the network rightly dislikes, and those visits leak into the target.

Further, the search relies on the value network's leaf evaluations; where those are inaccurate, the search amplifies the errors rather than averaging them out.

Danihelka et al. ("Policy improvement by planning with Gumbel", 2022) showed that AlphaZero can fail to improve the policy when not all root actions are visited, and proposed Gumbel AlphaZero/MuZero to guarantee improvement. Grill et al. (2020) similarly showed visit counts only approximate a regularised policy optimisation solution, poorly at low counts.

points.why: The response omits how early resignations remove late-game examples from the replay buffer.
The response says search amplifies leaf evaluation errors but does not explain how those errors propagate upward through backups and distort selection.
The response explicitly links too few simulations to noisy visit counts and failure to explore good moves.
quotes: With a small simulation budget relative to the number of legal moves, visit counts are coarse and noisy: many good moves get zero visits

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: In AlphaZero-style self-play, MCTS constructs its move distribution from normalized root visit counts, assuming tree search reliably improves upon the policy prior. That assumption breaks down in three common ways. First, search relies on the value network to evaluate leaf states; when value predictions are noisy, poorly calibrated, or misled by shallow tactical horizons, backed-up values override accurate policy priors and steer visits toward overestimated blunders. Second, when the simulation budget is small relative to the branching factor, discrete visit counts coarsely distort probabilities: unvisited moves collapse to zero probability regardless of their prior weight, and if an early sampled mediocre action scores above the default value assigned to unvisited siblings, search can lock onto it without ever evaluating stronger alternatives, violating policy improvement. Finally, self-play injects root Dirichlet noise and exploration bonuses to force trial of low-prior moves, plus temperature scaling during action selection. Because empirical visit counts tally cumulative exploration effort rather than final post-search action values, simulations spent refuting inferior moves remain in the output distribution, diluting an already accurate raw policy unless simulations are abundant.

noweb.answer: In self-play reinforcement learning, Monte Carlo tree search improves upon the raw policy network only when its value estimates and visit statistics are reliable, which often fails in practice. Because lookahead actively seeks high-scoring leaves, search can act like an adversarial optimizer against an imperfect value network, steering play toward unfamiliar states where the value head overestimates positions due to blind spots or out-of-distribution errors. Under small simulation budgets—typical in fast self-play—visit counts are also coarse and dominated by exploration. Root Dirichlet noise and PUCT exploration bonuses deliberately allocate simulations to inferior moves; before search converges, normalizing raw visit counts into a policy target shifts probability mass away from strong policy priors onto explored blunders, a pathology that motivated methods like Gumbel MuZero. Finally, because standard MCTS backs up sample averages rather than minimax values, early exploratory mistakes inside a sharp, forcing tactical line depress its mean value, causing search to abandon the winning move that the raw policy network initially preferred.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
MCTS only improves on the policy network if its value estimates are better than the prior, and in self-play that often isn't true. Search uses the value network to score leaf positions. Early in training, or in unfamiliar positions, that network is noisy or biased. Search then tends to favor exactly the moves whose values are overestimated, so it amplifies the network's mistakes instead of fixing them.

The training target is also a problem. AlphaZero-style systems learn from normalized visit counts, which are a poor policy estimate when the simulation budget is small. With few simulations, many moves get zero or one visit, so the distribution is coarse and noisy. It is also distorted by the exploration bonus in the selection formula, by Dirichlet noise at the root, and by first-play-urgency choices. Danihelka et al. (Gumbel MuZero, 2022) showed that this visit-count procedure doesn't guarantee policy improvement when not every action is visited. Grill et al. (2020) showed that visit counts only approximate a regularized policy-improvement step and drift from it at low simulation counts.

In those cases the raw prior can be the better target. Fixes include Gumbel-based action selection with completed Q-values and policy targets computed from Q-values rather than raw counts.

models.answer: In self-play reinforcement learning, Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) can produce a worse move distribution than the raw policy network for several interacting reasons. First, MCTS relies on the value network to evaluate leaf states; if the value network is inaccurate, poorly calibrated, or noisy—common early in training or in unfamiliar positions—backing up those flawed estimates corrupts action values and steers search away from strong moves the policy network already favors. Second, when the simulation budget is small relative to the branching factor, standard visit-count distributions become sparse and high-variance, zeroing out unvisited good moves while over-representing moves sampled only a few times. Third, exploration mechanisms such as root Dirichlet noise and PUCT exploration bonuses intentionally allocate visits to suboptimal actions, distorting the empirical visit-count policy. Because visit-count targets under PUCT do not guarantee monotonic policy improvement at low simulation budgets, MCTS can actively degrade the prior policy rather than refine it.

models.answer:
Monte Carlo tree search can make the move distribution worse because it reallocates probability using estimates that can be less reliable than the policy network’s prior. With a limited simulation budget, a promising move that starts with a low prior may get too few visits to show its value. Meanwhile, a move whose early positions receive overly optimistic value estimates can attract more simulations and end up with too much probability.

This matters because self-play systems often turn root visit counts into move probabilities. Those counts reflect where the search spent its budget, including exploration, as well as which moves looked best. If the raw policy already ranks moves well, a shallow search with inaccurate value estimates can push probability away from stronger moves. Search is an approximate policy improvement step, so it can hurt on individual positions even when it helps on average.
